A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REVEL task and DragStream method. All 22 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v3, including their appendices, support comparison. Rendered figures and equations resolve text-extraction difficulties.

before.justification: v1 reports original comparisons against adapted SG-I2V and DragVideo on 204 annotated clips, component and loss ablations, and qualitative results using Self-Forcing and CausVid.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds runtime measurements, hyperparameter experiments, and demonstrations involving complex streaming conditions and Wan2.1.

M1.justification: The core losses, ADSR and SFSO remain. However, v3 changes cached-history bounds from an L_c window to all preceding frames and describes the Gaussian center using the edited rather than handle region. Figure 3 and Appendix D retain sliding-window descriptions. The PDFs do not clearly establish whether these edits represent implemented procedure changes or documentation corrections.

E1.justification: The original 204-clip benchmark remains, but v3 adds distinct evaluation conditions: occlusion and re-emergence, objects leaving and re-entering view, conflicting text and drag instructions, physically implausible manipulations, and extended streaming histories. These substantially broaden the tested conditions in Sections 5.3–5.4 and Appendices O–R.

E2.justification: SG-I2V and DragVideo remain the competing methods in the retained main comparisons. New analyses reuse no-drag and ADSR controls already present in v1. Wan2.1 is an additional backbone demonstration, while the added DragNeXt discussion does not introduce an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix C.1 retains the original benchmark and default optimization settings. New experiments introduce per-frame timing, iteration counts of 0/2/3/4, neighboring-frame counts of 0/3/9/18, Gaussian-width sweeps, continuous versus discrete cutoff-frequency sampling, and a Wan2.1 configuration. These substantially expand the evaluation protocols without establishing reruns of the original comparisons.

E4.justification: v3 retains the existing component, loss, frequency and context analyses, then adds runtime–accuracy tradeoffs and sensitivity studies for neighboring-frame count, Gaussian width, frequency sets and iteration count. It also adds sustained-drag ADSR analysis and case studies of occlusion, prompt conflicts, implausible instructions and re-entry.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The latent mean and variance plots describe distribution drift, not uncertainty across experimental runs; the additional tables retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: The original results remain unchanged, including Figure 5's DragStream scores of 23.05 ObjMC, 552.39 FVD and 23.72 FID, and the loss-ablation table. New Tables 1 and 4–7 add runtime and sensitivity results, while Figures 8–10 and 17–21 add qualitative findings. Table 5's intended metric and Figure 20's continuous-drag duration are ambiguously reported.

T1.justification: The written conditioning assumption changes: Section 4.1's factorization and Equation 6's cached-history expressions start at frame 0 instead of a finite L_c window. This is a limited formal revision, although its implementation implications are unclear. The REVEL definition, objectives and ADSR mathematics remain; no new proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: introducing REVEL, addressing latent drift and context interference through training-free DragStream, and supporting integration with autoregressive VDMs. The additional experiments do not redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive applicability and limitation discussions absent from v1. It attributes occlusion handling to pretrained priors, prompt overriding to explicit latent modification, and failures under implausible instructions to conflicts with learned priors. It also discusses accumulated errors in long videos and extends the applicability discussion to bidirectional models.

D1.justification: v3 adds explicit code and named project-page links; v1 provides an anonymous demonstration link. It also reports H20 inference timings and explains saving object features before departure for later re-entry. The main PyTorch, optimizer, denoising and feature-extraction recipe remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds six references concerning diffusion acceleration, autoregressive motion control, memory and semantic alignment. It explicitly credits DragNeXt for operation formatting and notes its lack of streaming editing. These are limited additions to an otherwise retained research-positioning narrative.

P1.justification: Most retained prose, including the abstract, contributions, conclusion and earlier appendices, closely matches v1. Changes include local explanatory edits, author/contact formatting, acknowledgments, renaming Section 5.2 to Analysis, and adding subsections and appendices for the new studies. The existing narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual presentation with runtime and sensitivity tables and multi-frame displays for complex conditions, failures, bidirectional generation and long sequences. Figures 4–7 are placed alongside experimental discussion instead of on pages containing references. Earlier appendix figures are retained and renumbered, rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: The added latency measurements, sensitivity experiments and explicit failure cases make practical claims easier to assess than in v1. However, complex-scenario evidence remains mainly qualitative, and new reporting inconsistencies limit its strength: Table 5 labels values on the paper's FID scale as FVD, while Appendix Q claims over 20 seconds of continuous dragging but Figure 20 labels 12 seconds. The net gain in empirical transparency is useful but qualified.
